unblocks: FETCH_CONCURRENCY 1 -> 4-8, worth 40-65 minutes. This was the single highest-value open probe in the plan.

cost.note: 4 GiB sparse file, mounted and destroyed. No vendor, no network beyond the one test fetch.

why_this_probe_exists: The plan raised FETCH_CONCURRENCY only 'once W0-Cap closes', because the 4 GiB loopback's kernel ENOSPC is the REAL safety system for parallel fetch - the 1.10x-declared overrun check is only a refinement, and round 1 proved it cannot be trusted on 73 of 230 units whose declared sizes are sentinels. Round 1 also asserted megacmd was 'the only unkillable operation' and that timeout(1) cannot stop it. An untested cap is not a cap, so all four properties were measured rather than assumed.

1_the_cap_exists.test: 5 GiB write into a 4 GiB loopback, as the pipeline user (no sudo)
1_the_cap_exists.result: dd exit 1, stderr 'No space left on device'

2_the_cap_is_exact.test: compare bytes actually written against filesystem size
2_the_cap_is_exact.why_it_matters: A loopback that silently over-allocates is WORSE than none, because it would be trusted and wrong.

3_it_does_not_eat_the_throughput.test: 2 GiB dd with oflag=direct, loopback vs host, same machine, back to back
3_it_does_not_eat_the_throughput.verdict: PASS - and this is the measurement most likely to have reversed the design
3_it_does_not_eat_the_throughput.why_it_matters: Loopback is known to be slower than a direct write. If it capped throughput below the measured 41-53 MB/s network fetch rate, the speedup this probe unlocks would evaporate and the loopback would be net negative. At 169 MB/s it is 3-4x the network ceiling, so the cap costs nothing.
3_it_does_not_eat_the_throughput.note: this was the stated reversal risk in the probe's own header

4_it_fails_fast_under_real_traffic.test: loopback filled to 708 KiB free, then a real 378 MB per-file mega-get into it
4_it_fails_fast_under_real_traffic.error: Download failed. error code: Insufficient disk space
4_it_fails_fast_under_real_traffic.SIGNIFICANCE: This DIRECTLY CONTRADICTS the plan's stated premise. Round 1 recorded megacmd as 'the only unkillable operation' on the grounds that timeout(1) does not stop it and a probe silently pulled 4.0 GB that way. Against a full loopback it does NOT hang: it refuses in under a second with exit 232 and a legible reason. timeout(1) cannot stop it; the kernel can, and does.
4_it_fails_fast_under_real_traffic.better_than_expected: megacmd appears to PRE-CHECK free space and refuse before transferring (0/0 KB), rather than failing partway through a transfer. That is the safer of the two behaviours - no partial audio is ever produced by a full loopback.

5_recovery.result: 34 MiB written at 3.3 GB/s - the mount is usable again with no remount

TWO_THINGS_THIS_PROBE_MISSED_ON_THE_FIRS.note: The first run reported PASS on a test that had proved nothing. Recorded because a test that proves something else is not a pass, and this happened twice today.

defect_1.what: The loopback mounted ROOT-OWNED. mkfs.ext4 -m 0 clears reserved BLOCKS, not directory ownership. The pipeline runs as azureuser, so every non-sudo write failed with EACCES.
defect_1.how_it_fooled_me: Test 3 reported 'Permission denied' and test 5 reported mega-get exit 56 'Write not allowed'. Both read as cap behaviour. Both were the permission problem. The verdict function accepted them because it only checked for a hang, not for the failure mode being the one under test.
defect_1.fix: sudo chown $(id -u):$(id -g) $MNT && sudo chmod 775 $MNT immediately after mount, with a positive writability assertion before any test runs.

defect_2.what: The real-traffic test used a 47 KB probe file against a loopback that still had ~16 MiB free. The file simply fitted, and mega-get exited 0. That proved nothing about behaviour at the wall.
defect_2.fix: fill the loopback to under 1 MiB free, then fetch a 378 MB file that MUST hit the wall. Re-ran; exit 232 in 0s.

NEW REQUIREMENTS THIS PROBE ADDS_TO_THE_: chown + chmod 775 on the mount point IMMEDIATELY after mounting, with a positive `test -w` assertion before any fetch. Without it every fetch fails with EACCES while appearing to be a cap failure.
Reap partial files after a failed fetch. One 0-byte partial was left behind by the refused transfer.
Build and mount the loopback at PIPELINE START, not once. A loopback mount does not survive a reboot, so the runner must construct and mount it every run and assert writability before admitting work.

VERDICT.statement: The cap is real, exact, costs 1.7% throughput against a ceiling that is 3-4x above the network fetch rate, fails fast and legibly under real traffic without spilling to the host, and recovers without a remount.
VERDICT.action: FETCH_CONCURRENCY may be raised from 1 to 4-8. Expected saving 40-65 minutes. A watcher that kills and reaps stragglers remains required, because the cap stops the write but does not reap the process.
